props.title: P.S.

sections.content: P.S. represents a fascinating entry in the early 2000s wave of magical realism romance films, alongside 13 Going on 30 (2004) and The Lake House (2006). Laura Linney delivers a captivating performance as Louise Harrington, a Columbia University admissions officer who encounters a young artist seemingly reincarnated from her first love who died decades ago. Director Dylan Kidd follows up his sharp debut Roger Dodger (2002) with this more contemplative piece that explores second chances, grief, and the ways our past relationships shape our present choices.

sections.content: The film's exploration of age gaps and power dynamics in academia feels especially relevant today, though P.S. handles these themes with nuance rather than sensationalism. Topher Grace's performance as the younger F. Scott/Scott balances perfectly between innocent artistic prodigy and old soul, creating genuine chemistry with Linney that makes their unlikely connection believable. The film shares DNA with Somewhere in Time (1980) and Ghost (1990) in its suggestion that love can transcend traditional boundaries of time and space. SUBHEAD: Academic Setting and Power Dynamics

P.S. joins films like Mona Lisa Smile (2003) and The History Boys (2006) in examining the complex relationships within academic institutions. But where those films focus on teaching dynamics, P.S. uses the university setting to explore themes of gatekeeping, opportunity, and the ways institutions can both enable and restrict personal growth. The film's Columbia University backdrop provides rich metaphorical terrain for Louise's journey of self-discovery and questioning of life choices.
